mains-language/paper-a-indian-language.body:
What Paper A is

Paper A is one Indian language from the Eighth Schedule. It is 300 marks and three hours. It is qualifying: you need 25% (75/300), and the marks are not added to the merit list. Failing it ends the attempt, so it deserves a planned place in the timetable.

The 25% rule
The Commission evaluates Paper A and Paper B alongside the scored papers, but only candidates who reach 25% in each qualifying paper are considered for ranking. Treat 75/300 as a floor, not a target.

What the paper tests

  • Comprehension: read a passage and answer questions on its meaning, inference and vocabulary.
  • Precis: compress a passage to about one-third without losing its argument or tone.
  • Usage and vocabulary: grammar, sentence construction, idioms and word choice.
  • Short essays: organised writing on a general topic.
  • Translation: English to the chosen language and the chosen language to English.

The notification does not publish a fixed section-wise mark split. Prepare all five areas rather than optimising for a guessed weighting.

Choose your language

Each practice page gives you the script, the traps, a practice workbook and a script checker. The four low-resource pages also carry a model-generated sample passage, clearly labelled and script-checked.

How to use the pages

  1. Pick the language printed on your Paper A question paper.
  2. Do one comprehension and one precis task a week in that script.
  3. Translate the same English paragraph both ways; compare meaning, not word order.
  4. Use the script checker before you ask for feedback. It catches wrong-script paste, not grammar.
Labelling
The practice tasks on these pages are original study prompts, not UPSC previous-year questions. The model-generated samples are marked as such. Official question papers are linked from UPSC's previous-question-papers page; this site does not invent questions or answer keys.

mains-language/paper-b-english.body:
What Paper B is

Paper B is the English qualifying paper: 300 marks, three hours, and a 25% pass mark (75/300). The marks are not counted in the merit list. It is set at matriculation standard, but that means careful, formal English, not a literature paper and not a grammar quiz.

The 25% rule
A candidate who fails Paper B is not ranked, however well the scored papers went. Treat 75/300 as a floor.

What the syllabus lists

  • Comprehension of a given passage.
  • Precis writing.
  • Usage and vocabulary.
  • Short essays.

The syllabus does not list a separate translation section for Paper B. Check the current notification and the printed paper before you assume a section will appear.

Where marks are lost

  • A summary instead of a precis. A precis keeps the argument and the tone in about one-third of the words. Cutting sentences is not compression.
  • Informal register. Contractions, chatty asides and rhetorical questions belong in a blog, not in a qualifying paper.
  • Vocabulary guessed from sound. Use the context of the passage. If a word is not clear, say what the sentence is doing rather than inventing a definition.
  • An essay with no structure. A short essay still needs a beginning, two or three developed points and a close.
  • Leaving a section blank. Attempt every section, even briefly. An unanswered section is a guaranteed loss.

A four-week routine

  1. Week 1 — Comprehension and precis. One editorial a day. Read once for the claim, once for the structure. Write the precis without looking back.
  2. Week 2 — Usage and vocabulary. Twenty minutes a day on sentence correction, idioms and word choice. Keep one error log.
  3. Week 3 — Essays. Two 250-word essays. Underline the thesis and the topic sentence of each paragraph before you write.
  4. Week 4 — Full paper. Sit one full Paper B under three hours. Fix the section that ran over time.
Answer discipline
Write the answer, not the working. The examiner is checking control of English, so a clear short sentence beats a tangled long one.

mains-language/precis-writing.body:
What a precis is

A precis is a compressed restatement of a passage. It keeps the main claim, the supporting reasons and the tone, and it is normally about one-third of the original length. It is not a summary of every paragraph, and it is not a place for your opinion.

The one-third rule
One-third is a guide, not a law. The real test is whether a reader who has not seen the original can recover its argument from your precis.

A method that works under exam pressure

  1. Read once for the claim. What is the writer trying to establish?
  2. Read again for the structure. Mark the claim, the reasons, the example and the conclusion.
  3. Write in your own words. Do not copy whole sentences. Keep technical terms that have no synonym.
  4. Cut examples before reasons. An example supports a reason; the reason is what the precis must keep.
  5. Compare. Does your version preserve the claim, the reasons and the tone? If not, revise before you count words.

Comprehension: fact, inference and tone

  • Fact is stated in the passage. The answer should be traceable to a line.
  • Inference follows from the passage but is not stated in one sentence. Explain the step, not just the conclusion.
  • Tone is the writer's attitude: cautious, critical, optimistic, ironic. A tone question usually asks for a word and a reason.
  • Vocabulary in context asks what a word means in this sentence, not in a dictionary.

Common traps

  • Copying the first sentence and calling it a precis.
  • Keeping every example and dropping the main claim.
  • Adding your own view on the topic.
  • Writing a list of points instead of connected prose.
  • Changing the writer's cautious tone into a confident one.
Practice drill
Take a 350-word editorial. Write a 110–120 word precis. Then compare it with the original: did you keep the claim, the reasons and the tone? Repeat with a different passage the next day.

mains-language/translation.body:
Translation is meaning, not word order

Paper A asks for translation in both directions: English to your language and your language to English. The examiner is checking whether the meaning survives and whether the target sentence reads naturally. A literal sentence that preserves word order but breaks the target language loses more than a freer sentence that reads well.

The first rule
Translate the sentence, not the words. If a literal version is unnatural, rewrite it in the target language and check that the meaning has not changed.

English to your language

  • Split long sentences. English uses long clauses; many Indian languages prefer shorter clauses with clear connectives.
  • Choose natural word order. Do not preserve English subject-verb-object order if the target language normally does something else.
  • Keep technical terms consistent. If you translate a term once, use the same term throughout the passage.
  • Watch register. A newspaper editorial is formal; a quoted conversation may not be. Match the passage, not your personal style.

Your language to English

  • Avoid literal translation. A sentence that is grammatical in your language may sound wrong in English.
  • Use standard English collocations. "Take a decision" and "make a decision" are both understandable, but one is the natural choice in the register.
  • Keep tense and modality. Do not turn "may" into "will" or "should" into "must".
  • Do not add explanation. If the source is ambiguous, keep the ambiguity rather than inventing a detail.

Grammar traps that cost marks

  • Subject-verb agreement in long sentences.
  • Tense consistency across a paragraph.
  • Articles and prepositions in English (a, an, the, in, on, at).
  • Reported speech: backshift the tense when the reporting verb is in the past.
  • Modifiers: put the modifier next to the word it describes.

Back-translation

Translate your answer back into the source language without looking at the original. If the back-translation says something different, the first translation lost or added meaning. This is the fastest self-check you can do without a teacher.

Practice drill
Take one 100-word English editorial paragraph. Translate it into your language. Wait ten minutes. Translate it back into English. Compare the two English versions and mark every difference in meaning.

questions.text: A "false friend" is:

options.t: A word that looks similar in two languages but means something different
A grammar rule shared by two languages

questions.sol: False friends are words that look alike but differ in meaning; they cause silent translation errors.

questions.text: When translating an idiom, the best approach is usually to:

options.t: Use an equivalent idiom or plain meaning in the target language

questions.sol: Translate the meaning, not the words. Use an equivalent idiom if one exists; otherwise use plain language.
